Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord –Col 3:20.

Years ago, there was a boy named Joey who lived with his father and mother on the outskirts of a city. One day Joey’s father gave him a brand new red and white bike, which he had been wanting for a long time.

There was a big hill close to their house where the big boys in the neighborhood enjoyed riding their bikes. Joey’s father strictly forbade him from riding with the big boys on the hill, since it was too dangerous. Instead, he was only allowed to ride down the nice smooth sidewalk, past numerous houses, through a little alley, and then finally back to his house once again.

As the days and weeks went by, this began to lose its excitement. He watched enviously as the big boys walked their bikes up the hill almost directly in front of his house. At the top they would jump on their bikes, and with gleeful shouts, race down the hardtop road, swiftly turning onto the adjoining street at the bottom of the hill.

“Whee, here we come!” they would shout as they rushed by, leaving Joey to pedal calmly on around his little block again and again.

“Come on Joey!” the boys hollered. “Why don’t you come up with us? See what fun we are having! You are too scared,” they teased.

Joey was too embarrassed to tell them that his father had forbidden him since he was too little and might fall off his bike and hurt himself. The boys would have only made more fun of him, so he remained silent. How he wished he could go up and show his friends that he was not afraid. Joey thought, “Maybe if I would go down the hill just once, my dad would realize that I’m not so little after all. Then Dad would be proud of me and let me go down the hill with the big boys anytime I want to. Oh, how exciting that would be.” The very thought made his heart beat quickly in anticipation.

Joey did not need to wait very long for his opportunity. His father was going to be gone for a couple of days on business. Joey thought this would be his chance to prove to his dad that he was able to ride his bike with the big boys. With excitement and anticipation, he took his bike up the hill. He felt so grown-up in the big boys’ company. Surely his father was wrong! Now he would prove to everybody that he knew better than anyone else what he was able to do and not do.

With a run and a hop, he was on his bike. As the bike went faster and faster, he grabbed the handlebars more firmly. At that moment, one of the mischievous boys, coming up the hill, tossed a stone at Joey’s tire as he flew by. Joey swerved sharply to avoid the stone. Before he knew what was happening, he was sailing thru the air without his bike. He rolled and skidded and bumped, before coming to a painful stop. Joey was one big mess. His pants and shirt were torn. He had cuts and bruises on his hands, knees, and face. No more was he thinking of being a hero of the great biking hill. Our little, humbled “hero” of the hill was taken home to his mother, who sympathetically and lovingly washed and patched his wounds.

The next day Joey’s father returned home. When he saw the bandages on his son and the damaged bicycle, he guessed the story immediately. Joey’s bike was put away in storage for several weeks as punishment for his disobedience.

Joey sat on the curb as the boys raced down the hill, then on to the other street. Now Joey had no desire to sneak off and ride his bike with the big boys. He had learned his lesson—to always obey his father, even when he thought he knew better. He realized that his father was not trying to ruin his fun but instead he was trying to keep him safe.

When Joey was again allowed to ride his bike, he was quite content to ride peacefully around his little block of houses. From now on he was going to obey his father, not only in matters of safety, but in all things.

I barn, varen edra föräldrar lydige i all ting; ty det täckes väl Herranom. – Kol 3:20.

För många år sedan fanns det en pojke som hette Joey. Han bodde med sin far och mor i utkanten av en stad. En dag gav Joeys far honom en alldeles ny rödvit cykel som han länge hade önskat sig.

Nära deras hus låg en stor backe där de stora pojkarna i grannskapet tyckte om att cykla. Joeys far förbjöd honom strängt att cykla med de stora pojkarna i backen, eftersom det var för farligt. I stället fick han bara cykla längs den fina, släta trottoaren, förbi många hus, genom en liten gränd och sedan tillbaka hem igen.

Allteftersom dagarna och veckorna gick började det bli mindre roligt. Han såg avundsjukt på när de stora pojkarna ledde sina cyklar uppför backen, nästan rakt framför hans hus. Uppe på krönet hoppade de upp på cyklarna och, med glada rop, susade nerför den hårdgjorda vägen och svängde snabbt in på den anslutande gatan längst ner i backen.

”Tjoho, nu kommer vi!” ropade de när de for förbi, medan Joey lugnt trampade runt sitt lilla kvarter om och om igen.

”Kom igen, Joey!” ropade pojkarna. ”Varför följer du inte med oss upp? Se så roligt vi har! Du är för feg”, retades de.

Joey skämdes för mycket för att säga att hans far hade förbjudit honom eftersom han var för liten och kunde ramla av cykeln och skada sig. Pojkarna skulle bara ha retat honom ännu mer, så han teg. Vad han önskade att han kunde följa med upp och visa sina vänner att han inte var rädd. Joey tänkte: ”Kanske skulle pappa inse att jag inte är så liten längre, om jag bara åkte nerför backen en enda gång. Då skulle pappa vara stolt över mig och låta mig åka nerför backen med de stora pojkarna när jag ville. Åh, vad spännande det skulle vara.” Bara tanken fick hans hjärta att slå snabbt av förväntan.

Joey behövde inte vänta länge på sitt tillfälle. Hans far skulle vara bortrest i ett par dagar i jobbet. Joey tänkte att det här skulle bli hans chans att visa pappa att han kunde cykla med de stora pojkarna. Full av iver och förväntan tog han cykeln uppför backen. Han kände sig så vuxen i de stora pojkarnas sällskap. Hans far hade säkert fel! Nu skulle han bevisa för alla att han själv visste bättre än någon annan vad han kunde och inte kunde göra.

Med en löpning och ett hopp var han uppe på cykeln. När den rullade fortare och fortare grep han hårdare om styret. Just då kastade en av de busiga pojkarna, som var på väg uppför backen, en sten mot Joeys däck när han susade förbi. Joey väjde tvärt för att undvika stenen. Innan han förstod vad som hände flög han genom luften utan cykeln. Han rullade, gled och slog i marken innan han till slut stannade med en smärtsam duns. Joey var ett enda elände. Byxorna och skjortan var trasiga. Han hade skrapsår och blåmärken på händerna, knäna och i ansiktet. Han tänkte inte längre på att vara hjälten i den stora cykelbacken. Vår lille, ödmjukade ”hjälte” från backen bars hem till sin mor, som med medkänsla och kärlek tvättade och lade om hans sår.

Nästa dag kom Joeys far hem. När han såg bandagen på sin son och den skadade cykeln förstod han genast vad som hade hänt. Som straff för sin olydnad ställdes Joeys cykel undan i flera veckor.

Joey satt på trottoarkanten medan pojkarna susade nerför backen och vidare ut på den andra gatan. Nu ville Joey inte längre smita iväg och cykla med de stora pojkarna. Han hade lärt sig sin läxa – att alltid lyda sin far, även när han trodde att han visste bättre. Han insåg att hans far inte försökte förstöra det roliga för honom, utan försökte hålla honom trygg.

När Joey åter fick cykla var han ganska nöjd med att lugnt cykla runt bland husen i sitt lilla kvarter. Från och med nu skulle han lyda sin far, inte bara när det gällde säkerheten, utan i allting.

And he [Jesus] spake to them a parable; Behold the fig tree, and all the trees; When they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand. So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand –Luk 21:29-31.

Summer truly is upon us; and the trees have shot forth. What an interesting term for our modern-day English language, yet we still understand its meaning and have a mental picture of what is happening—the leaves pushing out from places that over winter were bare. For me, I think it is easier to have this mental picture since I have seen time-lapse videos of plants growing or sprouting to life.

Anyway, so much for that. What about the rest of this verse? (…when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.) Surely most of us continue to see the end of time approaching—the wars and rumors of wars, the earthquakes, the political upheaval in nation after nation, societies moving further and further away from God, and churches and families being ravished by sin and scandal.

We have God’s own promise that what we know and experience here on this earth was designed, created, and expected by Him to be only a temporary reality. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail –Heb 1:10-12.

The Prevailing Menace of Doubt & Fear

As we, as a church (FCF) and as a ministry (TBV), interact with numerous challenging situations (broken homes, struggling marriages, adopted children, faltering youth, immoral addictions, emotional struggles, and mental health issues) we repeatedly run into questions of doubt. “Why did this happen to me?” “Why doesn’t God change my circumstances?” “How can I trust God when all these painful things have happened to me?” “How can I surrender my life to God when He isn’t trustworthy?”

Most believers claim to trust God and believe His Word. The challenge that seems to come for each of us is two-fold. First, many of us tend to think that believing is primarily “feeling” instead of “choosing.” Secondly, many of us find it easy to believe what God says when it agrees with our experience, our thoughts, and our feelings; the problem arises when what the Scriptures say pushes on my will, my view, my belief, my experience, etc.

On the first point (believing=feeling) we have God’s clear answer from the Apostle Paul, for we walk by faith, not by sight: –2Co 5:7. On the second point the reality is that each of these struggles are a clear test of whether we will obey God rather than man (including ourselves), whether we will let God be true and every man a liar (including ourselves), and whether we will allow God to be the authority on all things or if we will still insist on our own will. Many of us claim (give lip service) to trust and believe God in all things, yet when we are faced with our own time of testing, we fail miserably (I know I have).

Additionally, many of us define our lifestyle of doubts and worry as being something normal, yet the Bible tells us to be anxious for nothing and to cast all our cares upon our Lord. Here the world has slowly deadened our senses to the clear teaching of the Scriptures, in that we have come to accept as normal that which God would have us to rise above. If we step back and consider the definition of “fear” as being on a spectrum, with some fear being quite minor and some being quite severe, we will see that many of our accepted patterns of behavior are outside of God’s perfect will for our lives. Doubt would be on the lesser end of the spectrum, with worry having a slightly stronger presence and effect, while panicking or being frantic would obviously cause much greater interference in our normal lives. Yet the truth is that each one of these is still in the family of “fear,” with the outcome being that we are allowing fear to control us and dictate our thoughts and behaviors. God’s will is that all His children would walk by faith instead of by fear.

God never gives us grace for any of our worries, nor for any future possible “what ifs”. God only gives us grace to go through what He is placing in front of us moment by moment. In the same way that a woman with child must go through the scary possibilities of the pain of childbirth, so likewise, all human beings must go through each circumstance that God decides is our lot in life. Nothing that we try to think or do (fear, worry, move, change our location, spend money, or ask others to intervene, etc.) will stop or change what God wills for our life. It is our choice to either accept or resist the inevitable in our lives.

The reality is this—each of us will either yield [our] members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin by believing the lies of Satan and continuing to allow fear to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions, OR we will yield [ourself] unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and our members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), by choosing to believe what God says in His Word and allowing faith to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions.

Here a balancing perspective needs to be brought in. This does not mean that we never wrestle with difficult situations—Jesus did in the Garden of Gethsemane. It also doesn’t mean that we never appeal to God or our authorities to consider changing our current painful situation—again, Jesus did. Rather, we are to be honest with God (like Jesus was) about the struggle of our heart, but then we need to eventually walk forward in obedience, by faith, with courage (like Jesus did).

Ongoing Support Needed

A big thank you to all who so faithfully continue to support the work of The Berean Voice. It is through the many prayers, emails and phone calls of encouragement and suggestions, and the financial contributions of many believers that we can continue to minister to the needs of others. As a non-profit ministry of the church, we do not charge for our material or services, therefore we rely entirely on the ongoing freewill offerings of God’s people. Please prayerfully consider how God would have you to partner with us in this work.

If you believe that God would have you support us financially, monthly support makes our work easier since most of our bills are monthly. However, if this doesn’t work as well for you that is fine. For your convenience there is a remittance envelope in the center of each copy of the magazine or you can go to our website www.bereanvoice.org and use the “donate” feature there for online donations. En hij [Jezus] sprak tot hen een gelijkenis: Kijk naar de vijgenboom en alle bomen. Wanneer ze nu uitlopen, zien jullie dat en weten jullie uit jezelf dat de zomer nu nabij is. Zo moeten ook jullie, wanneer jullie deze dingen zien gebeuren, weten dat het Koninkrijk van God nabij is –Luk 21:29-31.

De zomer is werkelijk aangebroken en de bomen zijn uitgelopen. Wat een interessante uitdrukking voor ons hedendaagse Engels, en toch begrijpen we nog steeds wat ermee wordt bedoeld en hebben we een beeld van wat er gebeurt: de bladeren die tevoorschijn komen op plaatsen die gedurende de winter kaal waren. Ik denk dat ik me dit beeld gemakkelijker kan voorstellen omdat ik time-lapsevideo’s heb gezien van planten die groeien of tot leven komen.

Hoe dan ook, genoeg daarover. Hoe zit het met de rest van dit vers? (…wanneer jullie deze dingen zien gebeuren, weten jullie dat het Koninkrijk van God nabij is.) De meesten van ons zien het einde der tijden toch steeds dichterbij komen: oorlogen en geruchten van oorlogen, aardbevingen, politieke omwentelingen in het ene land na het andere, samenlevingen die zich steeds verder van God verwijderen, en kerken en gezinnen die worden geteisterd door zonde en schandalen.

God heeft ons Zelf beloofd dat wat we hier op aarde kennen en ervaren, door Hem is ontworpen, geschapen en bedoeld als slechts een tijdelijke werkelijkheid. En: Gij, Heere! hebt in den beginne de aarde gegrond, en de hemelen zijn werken Uwer handen; Dezelve zullen vergaan, maar Gij blijft altijd, en zij zullen alle als een kleed verouden; En als een dekkleed zult Gij ze ineenrollen, en zij zullen veranderd worden; maar Gij zijt Dezelfde, en Uw jaren zullen niet ophouden. –Hebreeën 1:10-12.

De aanhoudende dreiging van twijfel en angst

Wanneer wij als kerk (FCF) en als bediening (TBV) met tal van moeilijke situaties te maken krijgen (gebroken gezinnen, huwelijken die het moeilijk hebben, geadopteerde kinderen, jongeren die wankelen, immorele verslavingen, emotionele problemen en mentale gezondheidsproblemen), stuiten we telkens weer op vragen en twijfel. ‘Waarom is mij dit overkomen?’ ‘Waarom verandert God mijn omstandigheden niet?’ ‘Hoe kan ik God vertrouwen als mij al deze pijnlijke dingen zijn overkomen?’ ‘Hoe kan ik mijn leven aan God overgeven als Hij niet te vertrouwen is?’

De meeste gelovigen zeggen dat ze God vertrouwen en in Zijn Woord geloven. De uitdaging waar ieder van ons mee te maken lijkt te krijgen, is tweeledig. Ten eerste denken velen van ons dat geloven vooral ‘voelen’ is in plaats van ‘kiezen’. Ten tweede vinden velen van ons het gemakkelijk te geloven wat God zegt wanneer dat overeenkomt met onze ervaring, onze gedachten en onze gevoelens; het probleem ontstaat wanneer wat de Schrift zegt druk uitoefent op mijn wil, mijn visie, mijn overtuiging, mijn ervaring, enzovoort.

Over het eerste punt (geloven = voelen) geeft God ons een duidelijk antwoord bij monde van de apostel Paulus: want wij wandelen door geloof, niet door aanschouwen: –2 Korinthe 5:7. Wat het tweede punt betreft, is de werkelijkheid dat elk van deze worstelingen een duidelijke toets is: zullen we God gehoorzamen in plaats van mensen (waaronder onszelf), zullen we God waarachtig laten zijn en ieder mens een leugenaar (waaronder onszelf), en zullen we God in alles als autoriteit erkennen, of blijven we op onze eigen wil staan? Velen van ons zeggen (geven lippendienst) dat we God in alles vertrouwen en geloven, maar wanneer we zelf op de proef worden gesteld, falen we jammerlijk (ik weet dat ik dat heb gedaan).

Daarnaast bestempelen velen van ons onze levensstijl van twijfel en bezorgdheid als iets normaals, terwijl de Bijbel ons zegt nergens bezorgd over te zijn en al onze zorgen op onze Heer te werpen. De wereld heeft hier onze gevoeligheid voor de duidelijke leer van de Schrift geleidelijk afgestompt, zodat we normaal zijn gaan vinden wat God wil dat we overwinnen. Als we afstand nemen en ‘angst’ zien als een spectrum, met enerzijds geringe en anderzijds ernstige angst, zullen we zien dat veel gedragspatronen die we hebben aanvaard buiten Gods volmaakte wil voor ons leven vallen. Twijfel staat aan de lichtere kant van het spectrum, bezorgdheid heeft een iets sterkere aanwezigheid en invloed, en paniek of opgejaagdheid zou uiteraard veel meer verstoring in ons gewone leven veroorzaken. Toch behoren al deze vormen tot de familie van ‘angst’, met als gevolg dat we angst toestaan ons te beheersen en onze gedachten en ons gedrag te sturen. Het is Gods wil dat al Zijn kinderen door geloof wandelen in plaats van door angst.

God geeft ons nooit genade voor onze zorgen, noch voor mogelijke ‘wat als’-scenario’s in de toekomst. God geeft ons alleen genade om, van moment tot moment, door te maken wat Hij voor ons plaatst. Zoals een zwangere vrouw de beangstigende mogelijkheden van de pijn bij de bevalling moet doorstaan, zo moeten alle mensen elke omstandigheid doormaken die God voor ons leven bepaalt. Niets wat we proberen te denken of te doen (bang zijn, ons zorgen maken, verhuizen, onze locatie veranderen, geld uitgeven of anderen vragen tussenbeide te komen, enzovoort) zal tegenhouden of veranderen wat God voor ons leven wil. We kunnen ervoor kiezen het onvermijdelijke in ons leven te aanvaarden of ons ertegen te verzetten.

De werkelijkheid is deze: ieder van ons zal óf zijn leden der zonde tot wapenen der ongerechtigheid stellen door de leugens van Satan te geloven en angst onze gedachten en handelingen te laten motiveren en sturen, óf we zullen onszelf Gode stellen, als uit de doden levend geworden zijnde, en onze leden Gode tot wapenen der gerechtigheid (Romeinen 6:13), door ervoor te kiezen te geloven wat God in Zijn Woord zegt en geloof onze gedachten en handelingen te laten motiveren en sturen.

Hier is een evenwichtig perspectief nodig. Dit betekent niet dat we nooit met moeilijke situaties worstelen—Jezus deed dat in de hof van Gethsémané. Het betekent ook niet dat we God of onze gezagsdragers nooit vragen onze huidige pijnlijke situatie te willen veranderen—ook dat deed Jezus. We moeten juist eerlijk tegenover God zijn (zoals Jezus was) over de worsteling in ons hart, maar vervolgens moeten we uiteindelijk in gehoorzaamheid, door geloof en met moed verdergaan (zoals Jezus deed).

Voortdurende steun nodig

Veel dank aan allen die het werk van The Berean Voice zo trouw blijven steunen. Dankzij de vele gebeden, bemoedigende en suggestieve e-mails en telefoontjes, en de financiële bijdragen van veel gelovigen kunnen we blijven voorzien in de behoeften van anderen. Als een non-profitbediening van de kerk brengen we niets in rekening voor ons materiaal of onze diensten. Daarom zijn we volledig afhankelijk van de voortdurende vrijwillige gaven van Gods volk. Overweeg alstublieft biddend hoe God wil dat u zich met ons in dit werk verbindt.

Als u gelooft dat God wil dat u ons financieel steunt, maakt maandelijkse steun ons werk gemakkelijker, omdat de meeste van onze rekeningen maandelijks komen. Maar als dat voor u niet goed uitkomt, is dat ook prima. Voor uw gemak vindt u in het midden van elk exemplaar van het tijdschrift een antwoordenvelop, of u kunt naar onze website www.bereanvoice.org gaan en daar de functie ‘doneren’ gebruiken om online een gift te doen. Hieronder vindt u ter overweging een geschatte uitsplitsing van onze behoeften.

Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord –Col 3:20.

Years ago, there was a boy named Joey who lived with his father and mother on the outskirts of a city. One day Joey’s father gave him a brand new red and white bike, which he had been wanting for a long time.

There was a big hill close to their house where the big boys in the neighborhood enjoyed riding their bikes. Joey’s father strictly forbade him from riding with the big boys on the hill, since it was too dangerous. Instead, he was only allowed to ride down the nice smooth sidewalk, past numerous houses, through a little alley, and then finally back to his house once again.

As the days and weeks went by, this began to lose its excitement. He watched enviously as the big boys walked their bikes up the hill almost directly in front of his house. At the top they would jump on their bikes, and with gleeful shouts, race down the hardtop road, swiftly turning onto the adjoining street at the bottom of the hill.

“Whee, here we come!” they would shout as they rushed by, leaving Joey to pedal calmly on around his little block again and again.

“Come on Joey!” the boys hollered. “Why don’t you come up with us? See what fun we are having! You are too scared,” they teased.

Joey was too embarrassed to tell them that his father had forbidden him since he was too little and might fall off his bike and hurt himself. The boys would have only made more fun of him, so he remained silent. How he wished he could go up and show his friends that he was not afraid. Joey thought, “Maybe if I would go down the hill just once, my dad would realize that I’m not so little after all. Then Dad would be proud of me and let me go down the hill with the big boys anytime I want to. Oh, how exciting that would be.” The very thought made his heart beat quickly in anticipation.

Joey did not need to wait very long for his opportunity. His father was going to be gone for a couple of days on business. Joey thought this would be his chance to prove to his dad that he was able to ride his bike with the big boys. With excitement and anticipation, he took his bike up the hill. He felt so grown-up in the big boys’ company. Surely his father was wrong! Now he would prove to everybody that he knew better than anyone else what he was able to do and not do.

With a run and a hop, he was on his bike. As the bike went faster and faster, he grabbed the handlebars more firmly. At that moment, one of the mischievous boys, coming up the hill, tossed a stone at Joey’s tire as he flew by. Joey swerved sharply to avoid the stone. Before he knew what was happening, he was sailing thru the air without his bike. He rolled and skidded and bumped, before coming to a painful stop. Joey was one big mess. His pants and shirt were torn. He had cuts and bruises on his hands, knees, and face. No more was he thinking of being a hero of the great biking hill. Our little, humbled “hero” of the hill was taken home to his mother, who sympathetically and lovingly washed and patched his wounds.

The next day Joey’s father returned home. When he saw the bandages on his son and the damaged bicycle, he guessed the story immediately. Joey’s bike was put away in storage for several weeks as punishment for his disobedience.

Joey sat on the curb as the boys raced down the hill, then on to the other street. Now Joey had no desire to sneak off and ride his bike with the big boys. He had learned his lesson—to always obey his father, even when he thought he knew better. He realized that his father was not trying to ruin his fun but instead he was trying to keep him safe.

When Joey was again allowed to ride his bike, he was quite content to ride peacefully around his little block of houses. From now on he was going to obey his father, not only in matters of safety, but in all things.

Ihr Kinder, seid gehorsam den Eltern in allen Dingen; denn das ist dem HErrn gefällig. –Kol 3:20.

Vor Jahren lebte ein Junge namens Joey mit seinem Vater und seiner Mutter am Stadtrand. Eines Tages schenkte Joeys Vater ihm ein brandneues rot-weißes Fahrrad, das er sich schon lange gewünscht hatte.

In der Nähe ihres Hauses gab es einen großen Hügel, auf dem die älteren Jungen aus der Nachbarschaft gern mit ihren Fahrrädern fuhren. Joeys Vater verbot ihm streng, mit den älteren Jungen den Hügel hinunterzufahren, da es zu gefährlich war. Stattdessen durfte er nur auf dem schönen, glatten Gehweg an zahlreichen Häusern vorbei, durch eine kleine Gasse und schließlich wieder zurück zu seinem Haus fahren.

Mit den Tagen und Wochen verlor das seinen Reiz. Neidisch beobachtete er, wie die älteren Jungen ihre Fahrräder den Hügel hinaufschoben, der fast direkt vor seinem Haus lag. Oben sprangen sie auf ihre Fahrräder und rasten mit freudigen Rufen die asphaltierte Straße hinunter, um am Fuß des Hügels rasch in die angrenzende Straße einzubiegen.

„Juhu, jetzt kommen wir!“, riefen sie, während sie vorbeisausten und Joey zurückließen, der immer wieder ganz ruhig um seinen kleinen Häuserblock radelte.

„Komm schon, Joey!“, riefen die Jungen. „Warum kommst du nicht mit uns hinauf? Sieh nur, wie viel Spaß wir haben! Du hast zu viel Angst“, neckten sie ihn.

Joey war es zu peinlich, ihnen zu sagen, dass sein Vater es ihm verboten hatte, weil er noch zu klein war und vom Fahrrad fallen und sich verletzen könnte. Die Jungen hätten sich nur noch mehr über ihn lustig gemacht, also schwieg er. Wie gern wäre er hinaufgefahren und hätte seinen Freunden gezeigt, dass er keine Angst hatte. Joey dachte: „Vielleicht würde mein Dad merken, dass ich gar nicht mehr so klein bin, wenn ich nur einmal den Hügel hinunterfahren würde. Dann wäre Dad stolz auf mich und ließe mich jederzeit mit den älteren Jungen den Hügel hinunterfahren. Ach, wie aufregend das wäre!“ Schon bei dem Gedanken daran klopfte sein Herz vor Vorfreude schneller.

Joey musste nicht lange auf seine Gelegenheit warten. Sein Vater musste für ein paar Tage geschäftlich verreisen. Joey dachte, das sei seine Chance, seinem Dad zu beweisen, dass er mit den älteren Jungen Fahrrad fahren konnte. Voller Aufregung und Vorfreude nahm er sein Fahrrad mit den Hügel hinauf. In der Gesellschaft der älteren Jungen fühlte er sich schon ganz erwachsen. Sein Vater lag bestimmt falsch! Jetzt würde er allen beweisen, dass er besser als jeder andere wusste, was er tun konnte und was nicht.

Mit einem Anlauf und einem Sprung saß er auf seinem Fahrrad. Als es immer schneller wurde, umfasste er den Lenker noch fester. In diesem Moment warf einer der frechen Jungen, der den Hügel hinaufkam, einen Stein nach Joeys Reifen, als Joey an ihm vorbeisauste. Joey riss das Fahrrad herum, um dem Stein auszuweichen. Ehe er wusste, was geschah, flog er ohne sein Fahrrad durch die Luft. Er überschlug sich, rutschte und stieß sich, bis er schmerzhaft zum Stillstand kam. Joey war ein einziges Häufchen Elend. Seine Hose und sein Hemd waren zerrissen. An Händen, Knien und im Gesicht hatte er Schürfwunden und blaue Flecken. Er dachte nicht mehr daran, der Held des großen Fahrrad-Hügels zu sein. Unser kleiner, gedemütigter „Held“ des Hügels wurde nach Hause zu seiner Mutter gebracht, die mitfühlend und liebevoll seine Wunden wusch und versorgte.

Am nächsten Tag kam Joeys Vater nach Hause zurück. Als er die Verbände an seinem Sohn und das beschädigte Fahrrad sah, erriet er sofort, was geschehen war. Zur Strafe für seinen Ungehorsam wurde Joeys Fahrrad für mehrere Wochen weggeräumt.

Joey saß am Straßenrand, während die Jungen den Hügel hinunter und dann weiter in die andere Straße rasten. Nun wollte Joey nicht mehr heimlich davonfahren und mit den älteren Jungen Fahrrad fahren. Er hatte seine Lektion gelernt: seinem Vater immer zu gehorchen, selbst wenn er meinte, es besser zu wissen. Er begriff, dass sein Vater ihm nicht den Spaß verderben wollte, sondern ihn beschützen wollte.

Als Joey wieder mit seinem Fahrrad fahren durfte, war er ganz zufrieden damit, friedlich um seinen kleinen Häuserblock zu radeln. Von nun an wollte er seinem Vater nicht nur in Fragen der Sicherheit gehorchen, sondern in allen Dingen.

And he [Jesus] spake to them a parable; Behold the fig tree, and all the trees; When they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand. So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand –Luk 21:29-31.

Summer truly is upon us; and the trees have shot forth. What an interesting term for our modern-day English language, yet we still understand its meaning and have a mental picture of what is happening—the leaves pushing out from places that over winter were bare. For me, I think it is easier to have this mental picture since I have seen time-lapse videos of plants growing or sprouting to life.

Anyway, so much for that. What about the rest of this verse? (…when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.) Surely most of us continue to see the end of time approaching—the wars and rumors of wars, the earthquakes, the political upheaval in nation after nation, societies moving further and further away from God, and churches and families being ravished by sin and scandal.

We have God’s own promise that what we know and experience here on this earth was designed, created, and expected by Him to be only a temporary reality. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail –Heb 1:10-12.

The Prevailing Menace of Doubt & Fear

As we, as a church (FCF) and as a ministry (TBV), interact with numerous challenging situations (broken homes, struggling marriages, adopted children, faltering youth, immoral addictions, emotional struggles, and mental health issues) we repeatedly run into questions of doubt. “Why did this happen to me?” “Why doesn’t God change my circumstances?” “How can I trust God when all these painful things have happened to me?” “How can I surrender my life to God when He isn’t trustworthy?”

Most believers claim to trust God and believe His Word. The challenge that seems to come for each of us is two-fold. First, many of us tend to think that believing is primarily “feeling” instead of “choosing.” Secondly, many of us find it easy to believe what God says when it agrees with our experience, our thoughts, and our feelings; the problem arises when what the Scriptures say pushes on my will, my view, my belief, my experience, etc.

On the first point (believing=feeling) we have God’s clear answer from the Apostle Paul, for we walk by faith, not by sight: –2Co 5:7. On the second point the reality is that each of these struggles are a clear test of whether we will obey God rather than man (including ourselves), whether we will let God be true and every man a liar (including ourselves), and whether we will allow God to be the authority on all things or if we will still insist on our own will. Many of us claim (give lip service) to trust and believe God in all things, yet when we are faced with our own time of testing, we fail miserably (I know I have).

Additionally, many of us define our lifestyle of doubts and worry as being something normal, yet the Bible tells us to be anxious for nothing and to cast all our cares upon our Lord. Here the world has slowly deadened our senses to the clear teaching of the Scriptures, in that we have come to accept as normal that which God would have us to rise above. If we step back and consider the definition of “fear” as being on a spectrum, with some fear being quite minor and some being quite severe, we will see that many of our accepted patterns of behavior are outside of God’s perfect will for our lives. Doubt would be on the lesser end of the spectrum, with worry having a slightly stronger presence and effect, while panicking or being frantic would obviously cause much greater interference in our normal lives. Yet the truth is that each one of these is still in the family of “fear,” with the outcome being that we are allowing fear to control us and dictate our thoughts and behaviors. God’s will is that all His children would walk by faith instead of by fear.

God never gives us grace for any of our worries, nor for any future possible “what ifs”. God only gives us grace to go through what He is placing in front of us moment by moment. In the same way that a woman with child must go through the scary possibilities of the pain of childbirth, so likewise, all human beings must go through each circumstance that God decides is our lot in life. Nothing that we try to think or do (fear, worry, move, change our location, spend money, or ask others to intervene, etc.) will stop or change what God wills for our life. It is our choice to either accept or resist the inevitable in our lives.

The reality is this—each of us will either yield [our] members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin by believing the lies of Satan and continuing to allow fear to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions, OR we will yield [ourself] unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and our members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), by choosing to believe what God says in His Word and allowing faith to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions.

Here a balancing perspective needs to be brought in. This does not mean that we never wrestle with difficult situations—Jesus did in the Garden of Gethsemane. It also doesn’t mean that we never appeal to God or our authorities to consider changing our current painful situation—again, Jesus did. Rather, we are to be honest with God (like Jesus was) about the struggle of our heart, but then we need to eventually walk forward in obedience, by faith, with courage (like Jesus did).

Ongoing Support Needed

A big thank you to all who so faithfully continue to support the work of The Berean Voice. It is through the many prayers, emails and phone calls of encouragement and suggestions, and the financial contributions of many believers that we can continue to minister to the needs of others. As a non-profit ministry of the church, we do not charge for our material or services, therefore we rely entirely on the ongoing freewill offerings of God’s people. Please prayerfully consider how God would have you to partner with us in this work.

If you believe that God would have you support us financially, monthly support makes our work easier since most of our bills are monthly. However, if this doesn’t work as well for you that is fine. For your convenience there is a remittance envelope in the center of each copy of the magazine or you can go to our website www.bereanvoice.org and use the “donate” feature there for online donations. Und er [Jesus] sagte ihnen ein Gleichnis: Seht den Feigenbaum und alle Bäume; wenn sie nun ausschlagen, so seht und erkennt ihr von selbst, dass der Sommer jetzt nahe ist. So auch ihr: Wenn ihr seht, dass dies geschieht, so erkennt, dass das Reich Gottes nahe ist – Lk 21:29-31.

Der Sommer ist tatsächlich da, und die Bäume haben ausgeschlagen. Was für ein interessanter Ausdruck in unserer heutigen englischen Sprache – und doch verstehen wir seine Bedeutung und haben ein inneres Bild davon, was geschieht: Die Blätter treiben an Stellen hervor, die über den Winter kahl waren. Ich glaube, dieses innere Bild fällt mir leichter, weil ich Zeitrafferaufnahmen von Pflanzen gesehen habe, die wachsen oder zu neuem Leben sprießen.

Wie dem auch sei, genug davon. Was ist mit dem Rest dieses Verses? (…wenn ihr seht, dass dies geschieht, so erkennt, dass das Reich Gottes nahe ist.) Sicherlich sehen die meisten von uns weiterhin, dass das Ende der Zeit näher rückt – Kriege und Kriegsgerüchte, Erdbeben, politische Umwälzungen in Land um Land, Gesellschaften, die sich immer weiter von Gott entfernen, und Kirchen und Familien, die von Sünde und Skandalen verwüstet werden.

Wir haben Gottes eigene Verheißung, dass das, was wir hier auf dieser Erde kennen und erfahren, von ihm so entworfen, geschaffen und vorgesehen wurde, dass es nur eine vorübergehende Wirklichkeit sein sollte. und: Du, HErr, hast von Anfang die Erde gegründet, und die Himmel sind deiner Hände Werk. Dieselbigen werden vergehen, du aber wirst bleiben; und sie werden alle veralten wie ein Kleid, und wie ein Gewand wirst du sie wandeln, und sie werden sich verwandeln. Du aber bist derselbige, und deine Jahre werden nicht aufhören. – Hebräer 1:10-12.

Die anhaltende Bedrohung durch Zweifel und Angst

Wenn wir als Kirche (FCF) und als Dienst (TBV) mit zahlreichen schwierigen Situationen zu tun haben (zerrüttete Familien, kriselnde Ehen, adoptierte Kinder, gefährdete Jugendliche, unmoralische Abhängigkeiten, emotionale Kämpfe und psychische Probleme), stoßen wir immer wieder auf Fragen voller Zweifel. „Warum ist mir das passiert?“ „Warum ändert Gott meine Umstände nicht?“ „Wie kann ich Gott vertrauen, wenn mir all diese schmerzlichen Dinge widerfahren sind?“ „Wie kann ich mein Leben Gott hingeben, wenn er nicht vertrauenswürdig ist?“

Die meisten Gläubigen sagen, dass sie Gott vertrauen und seinem Wort glauben. Die Herausforderung, vor der jeder von uns offenbar steht, ist zweifach. Erstens neigen viele von uns dazu, Glauben in erster Linie als „Gefühl“ statt als „Entscheidung“ zu betrachten. Zweitens fällt es vielen von uns leicht, dem zu glauben, was Gott sagt, wenn es mit unseren Erfahrungen, Gedanken und Gefühlen übereinstimmt; das Problem entsteht, wenn das, was die Schrift sagt, meinem Willen, meiner Sichtweise, meinem Glauben, meiner Erfahrung usw. zuwiderläuft.

Zum ersten Punkt (Glauben = Gefühl) gibt uns der Apostel Paulus Gottes klare Antwort: denn wir wandeln im Glauben und nicht im Schauen. – 2 Kor 5:7. Zum zweiten Punkt ist die Wirklichkeit, dass jeder dieser Kämpfe eine klare Prüfung dafür ist, ob wir Gott mehr gehorchen werden als Menschen (einschließlich uns selbst), ob wir Gott wahr sein lassen und jeden Menschen zum Lügner (einschließlich uns selbst) und ob wir Gott in allen Dingen als Autorität anerkennen oder weiterhin auf unserem eigenen Willen bestehen werden. Viele von uns behaupten (bekunden nur mit Worten), Gott in allen Dingen zu vertrauen und zu glauben, doch wenn wir selbst auf die Probe gestellt werden, versagen wir kläglich (ich weiß, dass es mir so ergangen ist).

Außerdem bezeichnen viele von uns ihren Lebensstil voller Zweifel und Sorgen als etwas Normales, doch die Bibel sagt uns, um nichts besorgt zu sein und alle unsere Sorgen auf unseren Herrn zu werfen. Die Welt hat hier unsere Sinne gegenüber der klaren Lehre der Schrift allmählich abgestumpft, sodass wir das als normal hinnehmen, wovon Gott möchte, dass wir uns darüber erheben. Wenn wir einen Schritt zurücktreten und „Angst“ als ein Spektrum betrachten, bei dem manche Angst eher geringfügig und manche sehr stark ist, werden wir erkennen, dass viele unserer als normal geltenden Verhaltensmuster außerhalb von Gottes vollkommenem Willen für unser Leben liegen. Zweifel lägen am schwächeren Ende des Spektrums, Sorgen hätten eine etwas stärkere Präsenz und Wirkung, während Panik oder völlige Aufgeregtheit offensichtlich viel stärker in unser normales Leben eingreifen würden. Doch die Wahrheit ist, dass all dies weiterhin zur Familie der „Angst“ gehört – mit dem Ergebnis, dass wir zulassen, dass Angst uns beherrscht und unsere Gedanken und unser Verhalten bestimmt. Gottes Wille ist, dass alle seine Kinder im Glauben statt in Angst wandeln.

Gott schenkt uns niemals Gnade für irgendwelche unserer Sorgen oder für mögliche „Was wäre, wenn“-Fragen in der Zukunft. Gott schenkt uns nur Gnade, um das zu durchstehen, was er uns Augenblick für Augenblick vor Augen stellt. So wie eine schwangere Frau die beängstigenden Möglichkeiten der Schmerzen bei der Geburt durchstehen muss, so müssen alle Menschen jede Situation durchstehen, die Gott für ihr Leben bestimmt. Nichts, was wir zu denken oder zu tun versuchen (Angst haben, uns sorgen, umziehen, unseren Wohnort wechseln, Geld ausgeben oder andere um Hilfe bitten usw.), wird verhindern oder ändern, was Gott für unser Leben will. Es ist unsere Entscheidung, das Unvermeidliche in unserem Leben entweder anzunehmen oder uns ihm zu widersetzen.

Die Wirklichkeit ist diese: Jeder von uns wird entweder seine Glieder der Sünde als Werkzeuge der Ungerechtigkeit hingeben, indem er den Lügen Satans glaubt und weiterhin zulässt, dass Angst seine Gedanken und Handlungen motiviert und lenkt, ODER wir werden uns Gott hingeben als solche, die aus den Toten lebendig geworden sind, und unsere Glieder Gott als Werkzeuge der Gerechtigkeit (Röm 6:13), indem wir uns entscheiden, dem zu glauben, was Gott in seinem Wort sagt, und Glauben unsere Gedanken und Handlungen motivieren und lenken lassen.

Hier ist eine ausgleichende Perspektive nötig. Das bedeutet nicht, dass wir niemals mit schwierigen Situationen ringen – Jesus tat es im Garten Gethsemane. Es bedeutet auch nicht, dass wir Gott oder unsere Autoritäten niemals bitten, eine Änderung unserer gegenwärtigen schmerzlichen Situation in Betracht zu ziehen – auch das tat Jesus. Vielmehr sollen wir Gott gegenüber ehrlich sein (wie Jesus es war) und von unserem inneren Kampf sprechen; doch schließlich müssen wir gehorsam, im Glauben und mutig vorangehen (wie Jesus es tat).

Weiterhin Unterstützung benötigt

Ein herzliches Dankeschön an alle, die die Arbeit von The Berean Voice so treu weiterhin unterstützen. Dank der vielen Gebete, ermutigenden E-Mails und Telefonanrufe sowie der Vorschläge und finanziellen Beiträge vieler Gläubiger können wir weiterhin den Bedürfnissen anderer dienen. Als gemeinnütziger Dienst der Kirche verlangen wir für unsere Materialien oder Dienste keine Gebühren; deshalb sind wir vollständig auf die fortlaufenden freiwilligen Gaben von Gottes Volk angewiesen. Bitte überlegt im Gebet, wie Gott möchte, dass ihr euch mit uns an dieser Arbeit beteiligt.

Wenn ihr glaubt, dass Gott möchte, dass ihr uns finanziell unterstützt, erleichtert eine monatliche Unterstützung unsere Arbeit, da die meisten unserer Rechnungen monatlich anfallen. Wenn das für euch jedoch nicht so gut passt, ist das auch in Ordnung. Zu eurer Bequemlichkeit findet ihr in der Mitte jedes Heftes der Zeitschrift einen Überweisungsschein; oder ihr könnt unsere Website www.bereanvoice.org besuchen und dort für Online-Spenden die Funktion „Spenden“ nutzen. Nachstehend findet ihr eine geschätzte Aufstellung unseres Bedarfs, über die ihr nachdenken könnt.

Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord –Col 3:20.

Years ago, there was a boy named Joey who lived with his father and mother on the outskirts of a city. One day Joey’s father gave him a brand new red and white bike, which he had been wanting for a long time.

There was a big hill close to their house where the big boys in the neighborhood enjoyed riding their bikes. Joey’s father strictly forbade him from riding with the big boys on the hill, since it was too dangerous. Instead, he was only allowed to ride down the nice smooth sidewalk, past numerous houses, through a little alley, and then finally back to his house once again.

As the days and weeks went by, this began to lose its excitement. He watched enviously as the big boys walked their bikes up the hill almost directly in front of his house. At the top they would jump on their bikes, and with gleeful shouts, race down the hardtop road, swiftly turning onto the adjoining street at the bottom of the hill.

“Whee, here we come!” they would shout as they rushed by, leaving Joey to pedal calmly on around his little block again and again.

“Come on Joey!” the boys hollered. “Why don’t you come up with us? See what fun we are having! You are too scared,” they teased.

Joey was too embarrassed to tell them that his father had forbidden him since he was too little and might fall off his bike and hurt himself. The boys would have only made more fun of him, so he remained silent. How he wished he could go up and show his friends that he was not afraid. Joey thought, “Maybe if I would go down the hill just once, my dad would realize that I’m not so little after all. Then Dad would be proud of me and let me go down the hill with the big boys anytime I want to. Oh, how exciting that would be.” The very thought made his heart beat quickly in anticipation.

Joey did not need to wait very long for his opportunity. His father was going to be gone for a couple of days on business. Joey thought this would be his chance to prove to his dad that he was able to ride his bike with the big boys. With excitement and anticipation, he took his bike up the hill. He felt so grown-up in the big boys’ company. Surely his father was wrong! Now he would prove to everybody that he knew better than anyone else what he was able to do and not do.

With a run and a hop, he was on his bike. As the bike went faster and faster, he grabbed the handlebars more firmly. At that moment, one of the mischievous boys, coming up the hill, tossed a stone at Joey’s tire as he flew by. Joey swerved sharply to avoid the stone. Before he knew what was happening, he was sailing thru the air without his bike. He rolled and skidded and bumped, before coming to a painful stop. Joey was one big mess. His pants and shirt were torn. He had cuts and bruises on his hands, knees, and face. No more was he thinking of being a hero of the great biking hill. Our little, humbled “hero” of the hill was taken home to his mother, who sympathetically and lovingly washed and patched his wounds.

The next day Joey’s father returned home. When he saw the bandages on his son and the damaged bicycle, he guessed the story immediately. Joey’s bike was put away in storage for several weeks as punishment for his disobedience.

Joey sat on the curb as the boys raced down the hill, then on to the other street. Now Joey had no desire to sneak off and ride his bike with the big boys. He had learned his lesson—to always obey his father, even when he thought he knew better. He realized that his father was not trying to ruin his fun but instead he was trying to keep him safe.

When Joey was again allowed to ride his bike, he was quite content to ride peacefully around his little block of houses. From now on he was going to obey his father, not only in matters of safety, but in all things.

Kinders, julle moet jul ouers in alles gehoorsaam wees, want dit is die Here welbehaaglik. –Kol 3:20.

Jare gelede was daar ’n seun met die naam Joey wat saam met sy pa en ma aan die buitewyke van ’n stad gewoon het. Eendag het Joey se pa vir hom ’n splinternuwe rooi-en-wit fiets gegee, waarna hy al lank verlang het.

Naby hulle huis was daar ’n groot heuwel waar die groot seuns in die buurt dit geniet het om met hulle fietse te ry. Joey se pa het hom streng verbied om saam met die groot seuns op die heuwel te ry, omdat dit te gevaarlik was. Hy is eerder net toegelaat om met sy fiets op die mooi, gladde sypaadjie af te ry, verby talle huise, deur ’n klein stegie en dan uiteindelik weer terug huis toe.

Namate die dae en weke verbygegaan het, het dit al minder opwindend geword. Hy het afgunstig toegekyk hoe die groot seuns hulle fietse teen die heuwel opstoot, amper reg voor sy huis. Bo-aan het hulle op hulle fietse gespring en met uitbundige uitroepe teen die teerpad af gejaag, terwyl hulle onder aan die heuwel vinnig by die aangrensende straat indraai.

“Joepie, hier kom ons!” het hulle geskree terwyl hulle verbyjaag en Joey rustig op sy fiets om en om sy klein blok huise laat trap het.

“Kom saam, Joey!” het die seuns geskree. “Hoekom kom jy nie saam met ons op nie? Kyk hoe lekker kuier ons! Jy is te bang,” het hulle hom gespot.

Joey was te skaam om vir hulle te sê dat sy pa hom verbied het omdat hy nog te klein was en dalk van sy fiets kon afval en seerkry. Die seuns sou hom net nog meer gespot het, daarom het hy stilgebly. Hoe graag wou hy nie opgaan en vir sy vriende wys dat hy nie bang was nie. Joey het gedink: “Miskien, as ek net een keer teen die heuwel af ry, sal Pa besef dat ek tog nie meer so klein is nie. Dan sal Pa trots wees op my en my toelaat om saam met die groot seuns teen die heuwel af te ry wanneer ek wil. O, hoe opwindend sal dit wees.” Net die gedagte daaraan het sy hart vinnig laat klop van opgewondenheid.

Joey hoef nie lank vir sy kans te wag nie. Sy pa sou ’n paar dae lank vir werk weg wees. Joey het gedink dit sou sy kans wees om vir sy pa te bewys dat hy saam met die groot seuns met sy fiets kon ry. Vol opgewondenheid en afwagting het hy sy fiets teen die heuwel uitgestoot. In die geselskap van die groot seuns het hy so groot gevoel. Sy pa was tog seker verkeerd! Nou sou hy vir almal bewys dat hy beter as enigiemand anders geweet het wat hy kon en nie kon doen nie.

Met ’n aanloop en ’n sprong was hy op sy fiets. Namate die fiets vinniger en vinniger beweeg het, het hy die handvatsels stewiger vasgegryp. Op daardie oomblik het een van die ondeunde seuns, wat teen die heuwel opgekom het, ’n klip na Joey se band gegooi terwyl hy verbygejaag het. Joey het skerp uitgeswaai om die klip te vermy. Voordat hy besef het wat gebeur, het hy sonder sy fiets deur die lug getrek. Hy het gerol, gegly en gestamp voordat hy pynlik tot stilstand gekom het. Joey was ’n deurmekaar spul. Sy broek en hemp was geskeur. Sy hande, knieë en gesig was vol snye en kneusplekke. Hy het nie meer daaraan gedink om die held van die groot fietsryheuwel te wees nie. Ons klein, vernederde “held” van die heuwel is huis toe geneem na sy ma, wat sy wonde simpatiek en liefdevol gewas en verbind het.

Die volgende dag het Joey se pa teruggekom huis toe. Toe hy die verbande aan sy seun en die beskadigde fiets sien, het hy dadelik geraai wat gebeur het. Joey se fiets is vir ’n paar weke as straf vir sy ongehoorsaamheid weggepak.

Joey het op die randsteen gesit terwyl die seuns teen die heuwel afjaag en dan verder na die ander straat toe ry. Nou wou Joey glad nie meer stilletjies wegsluip om saam met die groot seuns fiets te ry nie. Hy het sy les geleer: hy moes altyd sy pa gehoorsaam, selfs wanneer hy gedink het hy weet beter. Hy het besef dat sy pa nie sy pret probeer bederf het nie, maar hom eerder veilig probeer hou het.

Toe Joey weer toegelaat is om met sy fiets te ry, was hy heel tevrede om rustig om sy klein blok huise te ry. Van toe af sou hy sy pa gehoorsaam, nie net in veiligheidsake nie, maar in alles.

Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well pleasing unto the Lord –Col 3:20.

Years ago, there was a boy named Joey who lived with his father and mother on the outskirts of a city. One day Joey’s father gave him a brand new red and white bike, which he had been wanting for a long time.

There was a big hill close to their house where the big boys in the neighborhood enjoyed riding their bikes. Joey’s father strictly forbade him from riding with the big boys on the hill, since it was too dangerous. Instead, he was only allowed to ride down the nice smooth sidewalk, past numerous houses, through a little alley, and then finally back to his house once again.

As the days and weeks went by, this began to lose its excitement. He watched enviously as the big boys walked their bikes up the hill almost directly in front of his house. At the top they would jump on their bikes, and with gleeful shouts, race down the hardtop road, swiftly turning onto the adjoining street at the bottom of the hill.

“Whee, here we come!” they would shout as they rushed by, leaving Joey to pedal calmly on around his little block again and again.

“Come on Joey!” the boys hollered. “Why don’t you come up with us? See what fun we are having! You are too scared,” they teased.

Joey was too embarrassed to tell them that his father had forbidden him since he was too little and might fall off his bike and hurt himself. The boys would have only made more fun of him, so he remained silent. How he wished he could go up and show his friends that he was not afraid. Joey thought, “Maybe if I would go down the hill just once, my dad would realize that I’m not so little after all. Then Dad would be proud of me and let me go down the hill with the big boys anytime I want to. Oh, how exciting that would be.” The very thought made his heart beat quickly in anticipation.

Joey did not need to wait very long for his opportunity. His father was going to be gone for a couple of days on business. Joey thought this would be his chance to prove to his dad that he was able to ride his bike with the big boys. With excitement and anticipation, he took his bike up the hill. He felt so grown-up in the big boys’ company. Surely his father was wrong! Now he would prove to everybody that he knew better than anyone else what he was able to do and not do.

With a run and a hop, he was on his bike. As the bike went faster and faster, he grabbed the handlebars more firmly. At that moment, one of the mischievous boys, coming up the hill, tossed a stone at Joey’s tire as he flew by. Joey swerved sharply to avoid the stone. Before he knew what was happening, he was sailing thru the air without his bike. He rolled and skidded and bumped, before coming to a painful stop. Joey was one big mess. His pants and shirt were torn. He had cuts and bruises on his hands, knees, and face. No more was he thinking of being a hero of the great biking hill. Our little, humbled “hero” of the hill was taken home to his mother, who sympathetically and lovingly washed and patched his wounds.

The next day Joey’s father returned home. When he saw the bandages on his son and the damaged bicycle, he guessed the story immediately. Joey’s bike was put away in storage for several weeks as punishment for his disobedience.

Joey sat on the curb as the boys raced down the hill, then on to the other street. Now Joey had no desire to sneak off and ride his bike with the big boys. He had learned his lesson—to always obey his father, even when he thought he knew better. He realized that his father was not trying to ruin his fun but instead he was trying to keep him safe.

When Joey was again allowed to ride his bike, he was quite content to ride peacefully around his little block of houses. From now on he was going to obey his father, not only in matters of safety, but in all things.

أَيُّهَا ٱلْأَوْلَادُ، أَطِيعُوا وَالِدِيكُمْ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ لِأَنَّ هَذَا مَرْضِيٌّ فِي ٱلرَّبِّ. –كولوسي 3:20.

منذ سنوات، كان هناك صبي يُدعى جوي يعيش مع أبيه وأمه في ضواحي مدينة. وفي أحد الأيام، أهداه أبوه دراجة جديدة تمامًا حمراء وبيضاء، كان يتمنى الحصول عليها منذ وقت طويل.

كان هناك تل كبير بالقرب من منزلهم، يستمتع الأولاد الكبار في الحي بركوب دراجاتهم عليه. وقد منعه أبوه بشدة من ركوب دراجته مع الأولاد الكبار على التل، لأنه كان خطرًا جدًا. وبدلًا من ذلك، لم يُسمح له إلا بركوب دراجته على الرصيف الجميل الأملس، مارًا بعدد كبير من المنازل، وعبر زقاق صغير، ثم عائدًا أخيرًا إلى منزله مرة أخرى.

ومع مرور الأيام والأسابيع، بدأ الأمر يفقد متعته. كان يشاهد بحسد الأولاد الكبار وهم يدفعون دراجاتهم صعودًا إلى التل، الذي يقع تقريبًا أمام منزله مباشرة. وعند القمة، كانوا يركبون دراجاتهم، وينطلقون على الطريق المعبد وهم يصرخون فرحًا، ثم ينعطفون بسرعة إلى الشارع المتفرع عند أسفل التل.

كانوا يصيحون وهم يندفعون مارّين به: «هيّا، ها نحن قادمون!» فيتركون جوي يدوس بدراجته بهدوء حول مربعه الصغير مرة بعد مرة.

هتف الأولاد: «هيا يا جوي! لماذا لا تصعد معنا؟ انظر كم نستمتع! أنت خائف جدًا»، وسخروا منه.

كان جوي يشعر بإحراج شديد يمنعه من إخبارهم بأن أباه منعه من ذلك لأنه كان صغيرًا جدًا، وقد يسقط عن دراجته ويؤذي نفسه. ولم يكن الأولاد إلا ليسخروا منه أكثر، فظل صامتًا. كم تمنى لو استطاع الصعود وإظهار أنه غير خائف لأصدقائه. وفكر جوي: «ربما لو نزلت التل مرة واحدة فقط، فسيدرك أبي أنني لم أعد صغيرًا إلى هذا الحد. وعندئذ سيفتخر بي أبي ويسمح لي بالنزول على التل مع الأولاد الكبار متى أردت. آه، كم سيكون ذلك مثيرًا!» جعلته مجرد هذه الفكرة يشعر بأن قلبه يخفق بسرعة ترقبًا.

لم يحتج جوي إلى الانتظار طويلًا حتى سنحت له الفرصة. فقد كان أبوه سيغيب في رحلة عمل لبضعة أيام. وظن جوي أن هذه فرصته ليثبت لأبيه أنه يستطيع ركوب دراجته مع الأولاد الكبار. وبكل حماس وترقب، صعد بدراجته إلى أعلى التل. وشعر بأنه صار كبيرًا جدًا وهو بصحبة الأولاد الكبار. لا بد أن أباه كان مخطئًا! والآن سيثبت للجميع أنه يعرف أكثر من أي شخص آخر ما يستطيع فعله وما لا يستطيع.

وبعد أن ركض وقفز، صار على دراجته. وكلما ازدادت سرعة الدراجة، أمسك بالمقود بإحكام أكبر. في تلك اللحظة، ألقى أحد الأولاد المشاغبين، وهو صاعد التل، حجرًا على إطار دراجة جوي بينما كان يمر مسرعًا. انحرف جوي بشدة ليتجنب الحجر. وقبل أن يدرك ما يحدث، كان يطير في الهواء من دون دراجته. تدحرج وانزلق وارتطم بالأرض، قبل أن يتوقف متألمًا. صار جوي في حال يرثى لها. تمزق سرواله وقميصه، وأصيب بجروح وكدمات في يديه وركبتيه ووجهه. ولم يعد يفكر في أن يكون بطل تل الدراجات العظيم. أُخذ «بطل» التل الصغير المتواضع إلى البيت عند أمه، فغسلت جروحه وضمدتها بمحبة وتعاطف.

في اليوم التالي عاد أبو جوي إلى البيت. وعندما رأى الضمادات على ابنه والدراجة المتضررة، خمّن القصة على الفور. ووُضعت دراجة جوي في المخزن عدة أسابيع عقابًا له على عصيانه.

جلس جوي على حافة الرصيف بينما كان الأولاد يندفعون نزولًا عن التل، ثم يتابعون إلى الشارع الآخر. ولم تعد لدى جوي أي رغبة في التسلل وركوب دراجته مع الأولاد الكبار. لقد تعلم الدرس: أن يطيع أباه دائمًا، حتى عندما يظن أنه يعرف أكثر. وأدرك أن أباه لم يكن يحاول إفساد متعته، بل كان يحاول أن يحافظ على سلامته.

وعندما سُمح لجوي مرة أخرى بركوب دراجته، كان راضيًا تمامًا بأن يركب بهدوء حول مربع المنازل الصغير. ومن الآن فصاعدًا، سيطيع أباه، لا في أمور السلامة فحسب، بل في كل شيء.

And he [Jesus] spake to them a parable; Behold the fig tree, and all the trees; When they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand. So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand –Luk 21:29-31.

Summer truly is upon us; and the trees have shot forth. What an interesting term for our modern-day English language, yet we still understand its meaning and have a mental picture of what is happening—the leaves pushing out from places that over winter were bare. For me, I think it is easier to have this mental picture since I have seen time-lapse videos of plants growing or sprouting to life.

Anyway, so much for that. What about the rest of this verse? (…when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.) Surely most of us continue to see the end of time approaching—the wars and rumors of wars, the earthquakes, the political upheaval in nation after nation, societies moving further and further away from God, and churches and families being ravished by sin and scandal.

We have God’s own promise that what we know and experience here on this earth was designed, created, and expected by Him to be only a temporary reality. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail –Heb 1:10-12.

The Prevailing Menace of Doubt & Fear

As we, as a church (FCF) and as a ministry (TBV), interact with numerous challenging situations (broken homes, struggling marriages, adopted children, faltering youth, immoral addictions, emotional struggles, and mental health issues) we repeatedly run into questions of doubt. “Why did this happen to me?” “Why doesn’t God change my circumstances?” “How can I trust God when all these painful things have happened to me?” “How can I surrender my life to God when He isn’t trustworthy?”

Most believers claim to trust God and believe His Word. The challenge that seems to come for each of us is two-fold. First, many of us tend to think that believing is primarily “feeling” instead of “choosing.” Secondly, many of us find it easy to believe what God says when it agrees with our experience, our thoughts, and our feelings; the problem arises when what the Scriptures say pushes on my will, my view, my belief, my experience, etc.

On the first point (believing=feeling) we have God’s clear answer from the Apostle Paul, for we walk by faith, not by sight: –2Co 5:7. On the second point the reality is that each of these struggles are a clear test of whether we will obey God rather than man (including ourselves), whether we will let God be true and every man a liar (including ourselves), and whether we will allow God to be the authority on all things or if we will still insist on our own will. Many of us claim (give lip service) to trust and believe God in all things, yet when we are faced with our own time of testing, we fail miserably (I know I have).

Additionally, many of us define our lifestyle of doubts and worry as being something normal, yet the Bible tells us to be anxious for nothing and to cast all our cares upon our Lord. Here the world has slowly deadened our senses to the clear teaching of the Scriptures, in that we have come to accept as normal that which God would have us to rise above. If we step back and consider the definition of “fear” as being on a spectrum, with some fear being quite minor and some being quite severe, we will see that many of our accepted patterns of behavior are outside of God’s perfect will for our lives. Doubt would be on the lesser end of the spectrum, with worry having a slightly stronger presence and effect, while panicking or being frantic would obviously cause much greater interference in our normal lives. Yet the truth is that each one of these is still in the family of “fear,” with the outcome being that we are allowing fear to control us and dictate our thoughts and behaviors. God’s will is that all His children would walk by faith instead of by fear.

God never gives us grace for any of our worries, nor for any future possible “what ifs”. God only gives us grace to go through what He is placing in front of us moment by moment. In the same way that a woman with child must go through the scary possibilities of the pain of childbirth, so likewise, all human beings must go through each circumstance that God decides is our lot in life. Nothing that we try to think or do (fear, worry, move, change our location, spend money, or ask others to intervene, etc.) will stop or change what God wills for our life. It is our choice to either accept or resist the inevitable in our lives.

The reality is this—each of us will either yield [our] members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin by believing the lies of Satan and continuing to allow fear to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions, OR we will yield [ourself] unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and our members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), by choosing to believe what God says in His Word and allowing faith to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions.

Here a balancing perspective needs to be brought in. This does not mean that we never wrestle with difficult situations—Jesus did in the Garden of Gethsemane. It also doesn’t mean that we never appeal to God or our authorities to consider changing our current painful situation—again, Jesus did. Rather, we are to be honest with God (like Jesus was) about the struggle of our heart, but then we need to eventually walk forward in obedience, by faith, with courage (like Jesus did).

En Hy [Jesus] het vir hulle ’n gelykenis vertel: Kyk na die vyeboom en al die bome; wanneer hulle nou bot, sien en weet julle vanself dat die somer nou naby is. So moet julle ook, wanneer julle hierdie dinge sien gebeur, weet dat die koninkryk van God naby is –Luk 21:29-31.

Die somer is inderdaad hier; en die bome het gebot. Wat ’n interessante uitdrukking vir ons moderne Engelse taal, tog verstaan ons steeds die betekenis daarvan en vorm ons ’n geestelike beeld van wat gebeur—die blare wat uitkom op plekke wat gedurende die winter kaal was. Vir my is dit makliker om hierdie beeld voor oë te hê omdat ek tydverloopvideo’s gesien het van plante wat groei of begin uitspruit.

In elk geval, genoeg daaroor. Wat van die res van hierdie vers? (…wanneer julle hierdie dinge sien gebeur, weet julle dat die koninkryk van God naby is.) Die meeste van ons sien tog steeds hoe die einde van die tyd nader kom—die oorloë en gerugte van oorloë, die aardbewings, die politieke omwenteling in land ná land, samelewings wat al hoe verder van God af wegbeweeg, en kerke en gesinne wat deur sonde en skandale geteister word.

Ons het God se eie belofte dat dit wat ons hier op hierdie aarde ken en ervaar, deur Hom ontwerp en geskep is, en deur Hom bedoel is om slegs ’n tydelike werklikheid te wees. en: U, o Here, het in die begin die aarde gegrondves en die hemele is werke van u hande. Hulle sal vergaan, maar U bly; en hulle sal almal soos ’n kleed verslyt, en soos ’n mantel sal U hulle toerol, en hulle sal verander word, maar U is dieselfde, en u jare het geen einde nie. –Heb 1:10-12.

Die heersende bedreiging van twyfel en vrees

Wanneer ons as ’n kerk (FCF) en as ’n bediening (TBV) met talle uitdagende situasies te doen kry (gebroke huise, huwelike wat sukkel, aangenome kinders, jongmense wat wankel, onsedelike verslawings, emosionele worstelinge en geestesgesondheidskwessies), kom ons telkens op vrae oor twyfel af. “Waarom het dit met my gebeur?” “Waarom verander God nie my omstandighede nie?” “Hoe kan ek God vertrou wanneer al hierdie pynlike dinge met my gebeur het?” “Hoe kan ek my lewe aan God oorgee wanneer Hy nie betroubaar is nie?”

Die meeste gelowiges sê dat hulle God vertrou en sy Woord glo. Die uitdaging wat blykbaar vir elkeen van ons opduik, is tweeledig. Eerstens is baie van ons geneig om te dink dat glo hoofsaaklik ’n kwessie van “voel” is in plaas van “kies”. Tweedens vind baie van ons dit maklik om te glo wat God sê wanneer dit met ons ervaring, ons gedagtes en ons gevoelens ooreenstem; die probleem ontstaan wanneer dit wat die Skrif sê, druk uitoefen op my wil, my siening, my geloof, my ervaring, ens.

Oor die eerste punt (glo=voel) gee God se apostel Paulus vir ons ’n duidelike antwoord: want ons wandel deur geloof en nie deur aanskouing nie: –2Co 5:7. Wat die tweede punt betref, is die werklikheid dat elkeen van hierdie worstelinge ’n duidelike toets is of ons God eerder as mense (insluitend onsself) sal gehoorsaam, of ons God waaragtig en elke mens ’n leuenaar sal laat wees (insluitend onsself), en of ons God in alle dinge as die gesaghebbende sal erken en of ons steeds op ons eie wil sal aandring. Baie van ons beweer (bely dit net met die mond) dat ons God in alle dinge vertrou en glo, maar wanneer ons voor ons eie toetsingstyd te staan kom, misluk ons jammerlik (ek weet ek het).

Daarbenewens beskryf baie van ons ons leefwyse van twyfel en bekommernis as iets normaals, tog sê die Bybel vir ons om oor niks besorg te wees nie en om al ons sorge op ons Here te werp. Hier het die wêreld ons sintuie stadig afgestomp vir die duidelike lering van die Skrif, sodat ons begin aanvaar het as normaal dit waarbo God wil hê ons moet uitstyg. As ons terugstaan en die betekenis van “vrees” as ’n spektrum beskou, waar sommige vrees redelik gering is en ander redelik ernstig, sal ons sien dat baie van ons aanvaarde gedragspatrone buite God se volmaakte wil vir ons lewe val. Twyfel sou aan die mindere kant van die spektrum wees, met bekommernis wat ’n effens sterker teenwoordigheid en uitwerking het, terwyl paniek of histerie natuurlik ’n veel groter ontwrigting in ons normale lewens sou veroorsaak. Die waarheid is egter dat elkeen hiervan steeds deel is van die “vrees”-familie, met die gevolg dat ons vrees toelaat om ons te beheer en ons gedagtes en gedrag te bepaal. Dit is God se wil dat al sy kinders deur geloof in plaas van vrees wandel.

God gee ons nooit genade vir enige van ons bekommernisse of vir enige toekomstige moontlike “wat as”-scenario’s nie. God gee ons slegs genade om oomblik vir oomblik deur te maak wat Hy voor ons plaas. Net soos ’n swanger vrou deur die angswekkende moontlikhede van die geboortepyn moet gaan, so moet alle mense deur elke omstandigheid gaan wat God besluit ons lot in die lewe is. Niks wat ons probeer dink of doen (vrees, bekommer, trek, ons woonplek verander, geld bestee of ander vra om in te gryp, ens.) sal keer of verander wat God vir ons lewe wil nie. Dit is ons keuse om die onvermydelike in ons lewens te aanvaar of te weerstaan.

Die werklikheid is dit—elkeen van ons sal óf ons lede as werktuie van ongeregtigheid aan die sonde oorgee deur Satan se leuens te glo en voort te gaan om vrees toe te laat om ons gedagtes en dade aan te spoor en te rig, ÓF ons sal onsself aan God oorgee as mense wat uit die dode lewend geword het, en ons lede as werktuie van geregtigheid aan God (Rom 6:13), deur te kies om te glo wat God in sy Woord sê en toe te laat dat geloof ons gedagtes en dade aanspoor en rig.

Hier moet ’n perspektief wat balans bring, bygevoeg word. Dit beteken nie dat ons nooit met moeilike situasies worstel nie—Jesus het dit in die tuin van Getsemane gedoen. Dit beteken ook nie dat ons God of ons gesagsdraers nooit kan vra om dit te oorweeg om ons huidige pynlike situasie te verander nie—Jesus het dit ook gedoen. Ons moet eerder eerlik met God wees (soos Jesus was) oor die worsteling in ons hart, maar dan moet ons uiteindelik in gehoorsaamheid, deur geloof en met moed vorentoe gaan (soos Jesus gedoen het).

Voortgesette ondersteuning nodig

Baie dankie aan almal wat so getrou voortgaan om die werk van The Berean Voice te ondersteun. Dit is deur die vele gebede, e-posse en oproepe met bemoediging en voorstelle, en deur die finansiële bydraes van baie gelowiges, dat ons in die behoeftes van ander kan bly voorsien. As ’n nie-winsgewende bediening van die kerk vra ons nie betaling vir ons materiaal of dienste nie; daarom maak ons geheel en al staat op die voortgesette vrywillige gawes van God se mense. Oorweeg asseblief biddend hoe God wil hê dat julle saam met ons aan hierdie werk moet deelneem.

As jy glo dat God wil hê dat jy ons finansieel moet ondersteun, maak maandelikse ondersteuning ons werk makliker, aangesien die meeste van ons rekeninge maandeliks is. As dit egter nie so goed vir jou werk nie, is dit ook goed. Vir jou gerief is daar ’n koevert vir bydraes in die middel van elke tydskrifuitgawe, of jy kan na ons webwerf www.bereanvoice.org gaan en die “skenk”-funksie daar gebruik om aanlyn by te dra. Hieronder is ’n beraamde uiteensetting van ons behoeftes vir jou oorweging.

It’s a calling sublime
That merits my giving
Of talent and time
To grow in the glory
Of what He would make--
My Father, the King,
Will all ugliness take
Away from my heart,
That it tarnish no more
And bring me the jewels
That He has in store.

A princess of God!
It’s a calling to live
A life that to others
Around me would give
A diamond of hope,
A desire for God,
The truth of salvation
By Jesus’ shed blood.
A call to live godly
In Jesus Christ,
Adorned with His meekness
And clothed with His light.

And he [Jesus] spake to them a parable; Behold the fig tree, and all the trees; When they now shoot forth, ye see and know of your own selves that summer is now nigh at hand. So likewise ye, when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand –Luk 21:29-31.

Summer truly is upon us; and the trees have shot forth. What an interesting term for our modern-day English language, yet we still understand its meaning and have a mental picture of what is happening—the leaves pushing out from places that over winter were bare. For me, I think it is easier to have this mental picture since I have seen time-lapse videos of plants growing or sprouting to life.

Anyway, so much for that. What about the rest of this verse? (…when ye see these things come to pass, know ye that the kingdom of God is nigh at hand.) Surely most of us continue to see the end of time approaching—the wars and rumors of wars, the earthquakes, the political upheaval in nation after nation, societies moving further and further away from God, and churches and families being ravished by sin and scandal.

We have God’s own promise that what we know and experience here on this earth was designed, created, and expected by Him to be only a temporary reality. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail –Heb 1:10-12.

The Prevailing Menace of Doubt & Fear

As we, as a church (FCF) and as a ministry (TBV), interact with numerous challenging situations (broken homes, struggling marriages, adopted children, faltering youth, immoral addictions, emotional struggles, and mental health issues) we repeatedly run into questions of doubt. “Why did this happen to me?” “Why doesn’t God change my circumstances?” “How can I trust God when all these painful things have happened to me?” “How can I surrender my life to God when He isn’t trustworthy?”

Most believers claim to trust God and believe His Word. The challenge that seems to come for each of us is two-fold. First, many of us tend to think that believing is primarily “feeling” instead of “choosing.” Secondly, many of us find it easy to believe what God says when it agrees with our experience, our thoughts, and our feelings; the problem arises when what the Scriptures say pushes on my will, my view, my belief, my experience, etc.

On the first point (believing=feeling) we have God’s clear answer from the Apostle Paul, for we walk by faith, not by sight: –2Co 5:7. On the second point the reality is that each of these struggles are a clear test of whether we will obey God rather than man (including ourselves), whether we will let God be true and every man a liar (including ourselves), and whether we will allow God to be the authority on all things or if we will still insist on our own will. Many of us claim (give lip service) to trust and believe God in all things, yet when we are faced with our own time of testing, we fail miserably (I know I have).

Additionally, many of us define our lifestyle of doubts and worry as being something normal, yet the Bible tells us to be anxious for nothing and to cast all our cares upon our Lord. Here the world has slowly deadened our senses to the clear teaching of the Scriptures, in that we have come to accept as normal that which God would have us to rise above. If we step back and consider the definition of “fear” as being on a spectrum, with some fear being quite minor and some being quite severe, we will see that many of our accepted patterns of behavior are outside of God’s perfect will for our lives. Doubt would be on the lesser end of the spectrum, with worry having a slightly stronger presence and effect, while panicking or being frantic would obviously cause much greater interference in our normal lives. Yet the truth is that each one of these is still in the family of “fear,” with the outcome being that we are allowing fear to control us and dictate our thoughts and behaviors. God’s will is that all His children would walk by faith instead of by fear.

God never gives us grace for any of our worries, nor for any future possible “what ifs”. God only gives us grace to go through what He is placing in front of us moment by moment. In the same way that a woman with child must go through the scary possibilities of the pain of childbirth, so likewise, all human beings must go through each circumstance that God decides is our lot in life. Nothing that we try to think or do (fear, worry, move, change our location, spend money, or ask others to intervene, etc.) will stop or change what God wills for our life. It is our choice to either accept or resist the inevitable in our lives.

The reality is this—each of us will either yield [our] members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin by believing the lies of Satan and continuing to allow fear to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions, OR we will yield [ourself] unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and our members as instruments of righteousness unto God (Rom 6:13), by choosing to believe what God says in His Word and allowing faith to motivate and direct our thoughts and actions.

Here a balancing perspective needs to be brought in. This does not mean that we never wrestle with difficult situations—Jesus did in the Garden of Gethsemane. It also doesn’t mean that we never appeal to God or our authorities to consider changing our current painful situation—again, Jesus did. Rather, we are to be honest with God (like Jesus was) about the struggle of our heart, but then we need to eventually walk forward in obedience, by faith, with courage (like Jesus did).

Ongoing Support Needed

A big thank you to all who so faithfully continue to support the work of The Berean Voice. It is through the many prayers, emails and phone calls of encouragement and suggestions, and the financial contributions of many believers that we can continue to minister to the needs of others. As a non-profit ministry of the church, we do not charge for our material or services, therefore we rely entirely on the ongoing freewill offerings of God’s people. Please prayerfully consider how God would have you to partner with us in this work.

If you believe that God would have you support us financially, monthly support makes our work easier since most of our bills are monthly. However, if this doesn’t work as well for you that is fine. For your convenience there is a remittance envelope in the center of each copy of the magazine or you can go to our website www.bereanvoice.org and use the “donate” feature there for online donations.
